                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                  §            OF TEXAS


      COMMENTS OF MONARCH ENERGY DEVELOPMENT LLC ON STAFF’s
           PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194

       COMES NOW Monarch Energy Development LLC (Monarch) and files these comments

regarding Commission Staff’s Proposal for Publication (PFP) of new 16 Texas Administrative

Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards, which would set forth the

standards and criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT

transmission network. The Commission is expected to consider the PFP at its March 12, 2026,

Open Meeting. Monarch has significant concerns that Staff’s proposal will obstruct development

of large load projects and respectfully requests that the Commission consider changes to the PFP

prior to formal publication for comment under the Administrative Procedures Act.

       Monarch develops industrial sites that can host a range of assets, including large loads.

Monarch Energy secures land, power, water rights, permits, designs, equipment, and other critical

development items necessary for bringing energy assets to communities. Monarch streamlines

development timelines for industrial-scale infrastructure, hyperscalers, cloud providers, and

enterprise operators.

       A significant portion of data center capacity is developed by independent data center

developers and operators that provide the physical infrastructure necessary to support future end

users. These independent developers are typically the entities responsible for managing large load

interconnection processes, including submitting interconnection requests, procuring equipment,
 coordinating with transmission service providers (TSPs), and bearing substantial up-front financial

and operational risk associated with interconnecting large loads to the transmission system.

       This development model benefits the market by producing market-ready projects that can

be offered to a wide range of creditworthy end users once infrastructure and interconnection

milestones are achieved. As a result, the entities that assume the primary financial, operational,

and interconnection risks associated with developing large loads frequently differ from the ultimate

beneficiaries of the projects that are constructed and occupied. This distinction is important for

consideration as we evaluate and implement new rules governing the interconnection of large

loads, including requirements related to security, risk allocation, and refund mechanisms under

Senate Bill 6.

                                          COMMENTS

1.     The Commission should clarify that large load interconnection projects that have
       already signed interconnection agreements and posted financial security are not going
       to be retroactively subject to a new set of rules.

       Monarch and other developers who have been diligently working with TSPs and ERCOT

to interconnect large load projects for several years should not be subject to retroactive

requirements that will essentially reject all progress and investments that have been made on

projects, such as where there already is a signed Letter of Authorization (LOA) and financial

security has been posted. While the objective of the PFP is to create more structure and

transparency around the interconnection process and weed out speculative projects, we

recommend that the Commission avoid erecting new barriers to projects that already are well

underway. For example, projects that already signed an LOA with a TSP to proceed with

construction of interconnection facilities and paid requested contribution in aid to construction

(CIAC) before the effective date of SB 6 (June 20, 2025), should not be retroactively subject to a



                                                                 Monarch Energy Comments - Page 2
 new set of rules that could undermine all investments made to date. To do so would be a perverse

consequence of these proposed new rules.

2.      Large loads should have more options regarding how to demonstrate site control at
        the Intermediate Agreement phase.

        Staff’s paragraph (d)(1) of the PFP would require large loads to have in place an extended

lease agreement or deed to property prior to an interconnection study being conducted. Requiring

this level of site control before the large load even has a determination from ERCOT as to the

potential for interconnection of the proposed customer at the site is premature and not

commercially reasonable due to costs of acquiring this level of site control. Monarch recommends

that, if the Commission deems it essential to demonstrate site control at this early phase of the

process, such demonstration should also allow for the use of a county recorded Purchase and Sale

Agreement. This approach is generally used for large industrial developments, including for the

development of new generation resources, and is in line with other markets such as SPP. Monarch

does not object to the more limited options of demonstrating site control at the Interconnection

Agreement phase of the process. However, as proposed, paragraph (d)(1) is overly prescriptive,

premature, would impose unnecessary costs on developers, and discourage the development of

data center facilities in Texas.

3.      The intermediate stage $100,000/MW financial security should be fully refundable
        after the payment of actual costs prudently incurred.

        Pursuant to proposed paragraph (g)(3), the PFP would allow the TSP to retain up to 80%

of the balance of financial security posted by the large load during the intermediate phase if the

load reduces or withdraws its proposed project. Monarch understands that the premise for requiring

the posting of this amount of financial security is intended to ensure that proposed projects are

“real.” But as proposed in the PFP, the financial security requirement acts as a penalty to deter the

development of “real” projects since the mostly non-refundable nature of this financial security is

                                                                 Monarch Energy Comments - Page 3
 arbitrary and not connected to actual costs incurred. This financial security should be fully

refundable after payment for actual costs that are prudently incurred in this phase of the process.

4.     Large loads seeking to interconnect should not be subject to pancaking of multiple
       non-refundable charges.

       As drafted, it is unclear whether the Staff’s PFP would require the $100,000/MW at the

intermediate agreement phase, and then an additional $100,000/MW at the interconnection

agreement phase, plus CIAC, plus financial security for system upgrades, plus financial security

on long lead equipment, and plus land purchases for site control. If loads are subjected to pancaking

of multiple non-refundable charges that exceed the actual costs incurred by a TSP, interconnection

projects will no longer be economic, chilling investment in Texas. As an example, if the

requirements of all the above were applied to a 500 MW large load project, the proposed

requirements would impose upfront costs of approximately $100,000,000 that are mostly non-

refundable before there is any certainty on allocated MW volume or energization date. This is a

strong deterrent to economic development in Texas and the ERCOT market. In order to protect

Texas customers from the cost of developing these new large loads, financial security that is

required to be posted should be linked to actual cost causation for the proposed projects, with

timing aligned to study outcomes and specific, identified upgrades needed to accommodate such

projects.

       We note that in Project No. 58480, Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting

Criteria Under PURA §37.0561, the Commission recently adopted criteria related to financial

commitment in which loads would be subject to posting of $100,000/MW of contracted peak

demand, posting of financial security for equipment with a lead time of at least six months, or




                                                                 Monarch Energy Comments - Page 4
 payment of CIAC for costs directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer. 1 This

approach is more reasonable than creating a set of pancaking requirements which would be

financially burdensome and could kill development of otherwise valid projects.

                                         CONCLUSION

       Monarch appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and encourages the

Commission to move to formal publication of a proposed rule with modifications consistent with

these comments.

                                                     Respectfully submitted,


                                                     ______/s/ Kevin Boudreaux____________
                                                                              Kevin Boudreaux
                                                                         Head of Power Supply
                                                             Monarch Energy Development LLC
                                                                       1460 Springrock Lane #4
                                                                            Houston, TX 77055
                                                                                (832) 875-0969
                                                                 KBoudreaux@monarch.energy

                                                                                    March 4, 2026




1
    Project No. 58480, Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting Criteria Under PURA §37.0561,
    (Feb.6, 2026) at 92.
